senses: (A child's name for) an elephant.
Something that is elusive.
ety: Probably a childish mispronunciation of elephant, perhaps influenced by half a lump (as in "I'll have half a lump of sugar in my tea"), coined by the English author Alan Alexander Milne (1882–1956) as the name of an imaginary animal in his book Winnie-the-Pooh (1926). The animal was not described in the book, but the illustrator Ernest Howard Shepard (1879–1976) depicted it as an elephant. Sense 2 (“something which is elusive”) refers to the fact that in Milne’s book the characters Winnie-the-Pooh and Piglet set a trap for, but are unable to capture, a heffalump.
examples: We went to the zoo and saw some heffalumps.
Yeees, we're going to the zoo to see animals. There are lions and tiggers and snakes and heffalumps.

senses: A petroleum-based thin and colourless fuel oil.
Paraffin wax.
ety: From Latin paraffinum, from parum (too little) + affinis (related, affinity). Therefore low affinity or being chemically neutral.
examples: She poured paraffin on the dry floors and on the pandanus-mats, and then she set fire.

The paper found high levels of phased-out flame retardants like PCBs and PBDEs, as well as allegedly safe, newer replacements chemicals, such as chlorinated paraffins and organophosphates, across the globe.

senses: Foul-smelling, stinking.
ety: Borrowed from Latin fētidus (“having offensive odour”), originally fēteō (“to stink”).
examples: I caught the fetid odor of dirty socks.

senses: Suggestive of a grave or of death; gloomy; solemn.
Having a hollow and deep sound.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin sepulcralis.
examples: He alluded constantly to Europe, to the people I was supposed to know there - putting leading questions as to my acquaintances in the sepulchral city, and so on.

senses: One whose parents were Japanese immigrants, especially to North or South America.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 二世 (にせい, nisei), from 二 (ni-, “second”) + 世 (sei, “generation”).
examples: Born and brought tip mostly in South America, the United States (particularly Hawaii) and Canada, the nisei and sansei have Japanese features but often speak the language imperfectly, if at all.
The Nisei, on the other hand, are more inclined to view the hyphenated Japanese Canadian identity with positive implications.
Decrypts fly out of a line printer on the other end and are taken off to another hut where American nisei, and some white men trained in Nipponese, translate them.

senses: A type of scrubland with low-growing thick eucalypts, characteristic of certain parts of Australia.
Any semi-desert region of Australia where such scrub is the predominant vegetation.
Any of several low-growing eucalypts characteristic of such scrubland, especially Eucalyptus dumosa, Eucalyptus oleosa, and Eucalyptus socialis.
ety: Probably borrowed from Wemba-Wemba mali; compare Woiwurrung mali.
examples: Although not totally destitute of animal life, in the summer season very few living creatures, beyond innumerable tribes of insects, are to be found within the Mallee.
It made no difference that he had also invented several ploughs and a device for grubbing Mallee country or that people had journeyed all the way from Melbourne to inspect them.
From the mallee and kurrajong trees came a rowdy chatter of parakeets, while queer soughing of air-currents came from the valley top.

senses: To occur afterwards, as a result or effect.
ety: From Old French ensu-, stem of some conjugated forms of ensuivre (“follow close upon, come afterward”) (French ensuivre), from Latin īnsequere, from īnsequi (“to pursue, follow, follow after; come next”), from in- (“upon”) (see in-) + sequi (“follow”) (see sequel).
examples: Give three freshmen six bottles of wine, and hilarity will ensue.

senses: A form of carbonized ancient plants; the hardest and cleanest-burning of all the coals.
A dark grey color.
ety: Via Latin from Ancient Greek ἀνθρακῖτις (anthrakîtis, “a kind of coal”), from ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “charcoal”). By surface analysis, anthrac- + -ite.
examples: In the past, when the author was studying, architects only employed a very restricted palette of colours: the white of modernism, black, a “friendly” shade of anthracite and light grey!

senses: Lukewarm; neither warm nor cool.
Uninterested; exhibiting little passion or eagerness; lukewarm.
ety: Borrowed from Latin tepidus. Cognate with Sanskrit तप् (tap), Proto-Slavic *teplъ.
examples: I'm drinking a cup of tepid water.
He gave me a tepid response to the proposal.

senses: A seaweed of a reddish-brown color (Palmaria palmata) which is sometimes eaten, as in Scotland.
ety: Borrowed from Irish duileasc, Scottish Gaelic duileasg; compare Welsh delysg.
examples: Then Egil said, ‘That happens if you eat dulse, it makes you even thirstier.’

senses: The supposed ability to detect whether or not a person is gay by observing that person's appearance, mannerisms, etc.
ety: Blend of gay + radar, equivalent to gay + -dar.
examples: This is not your Hallmark in Ames, Iowa. And there is “family” working there … no radar like gaydar, I always say.
When you first come out, you might have an overactive gaydar. When I realized I was gay, I wanted everyone to be gay too, which led to a lot of wishful thinking. "Helen Hunt is gay!" Dream on, girl!

senses: Financial technology, that is, technology (usually information technology) that is focused on finance.
A company in the finance sector, such as one dealing with payments, fundraising or loans.
ety: A clipping of finance technology.
examples: Fintech was every banker’s buzzword at the World Economic Forum.
Nubank is a fintech that was founded in 2013 and entered the Brazilian market to compete with traditional financial services providers.

senses: A robust container for fuel or water, of a certain more or less rectangular shape, often made from pressed steel.
ety: From Jerry (“a German”) + can, from its use by German troops in World War II.
examples: The police fell back, swatting and cursing. At the gateway, somebody grabbed a jerrycan of water from Jonamon's hut and flung its contents at the swarm.
Anyone with half a brain and a jerrycan of fertilizer's got an army.

senses: To defeat decisively, to suppress.
ety: From Middle English quaschen, quasshen, cwessen, quassen, from Old French quasser, from Latin quassāre, under the influence of cassō (“to annul”), from Latin quatiō (“to shake”) Cognate with Dutch kwetsen (“to hurt, injure”), German quetschen (“to crush, squash”), Spanish quejar (“to complain”).
examples: The army quashed the rebellion.
Contrition is apt to quash or allay all worldly grief.
Anne that she had been perfectly right in her proceedings, since, by quashing all idle hopes, both parties would see the necessity of conquering their foolish passion.

senses: A public hall designed for lectures, readings, or concerts.
A school, especially European, at a stage between elementary school and college, a lycée.
An association for literary improvement.
ety: From Latin Lyceum, from Ancient Greek Λύκειον (Lúkeion) (the name of a gymnasium, or athletic training facility, near Athens where Aristotle established his school), from Λύκειος, from Proto-Greek *λύκη), "light." The meaning of the epithet "Lyceus" later became associated with Apollo's mother Leto, who was the patron goddess of Lycia (Λυκία) and who was identified with the wolf (λύκος). Doublet of lycée and Lyceum.
examples: At a lyceum, not long since, I felt that the lecturer had chosen a theme too foreign to himself, and so failed to interest me as much as he might have done.
We burst out laughing. She told me that one of her teachers at the "lyceum" used to say that whenever any of the students got up to anything.

senses: A device for punishment. See bilboes.
A kind of sword with well-tempered and flexible blade, originally produced in Bilbao.
ety: From Bilbao, a city in Spain.
examples: A boy bursts in to the tent, double-edged bilbo in hand.

senses: A domesticated subspecies of water buffalo, Bubalus bubalis carabanesis.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish carabao, from Waray-Waray karabaw, from Malay kerbau, from Proto-Malayic *kAr(ə)baw, ultimately from Proto-Mon-Khmer *krpiʔ ~ *krpiiw ~ *krpuʔ ~ *(kr)puh (“buffalo”). Compare Khmer ក្របី (krɑɑbəy), Halang kơpùa, Indonesian kerbau, Javanese ꦏꦼꦧꦺꦴ (kebo), Thai กระบือ (grà-bʉʉ).
examples: The weaker carabaos are slaughtered for meat, the stronger ones put to work on Golgotha, and the drivers are assimilated into the workforce.

senses: One who or that which walks or goes; a goer; a walker.
A horse that goes quickly.
One who oversees a gang of workmen.
One who is employed in conveying the coal through the gangways.
ety: From Middle English ganger, from Old English gangere (“a ganger, footman”), equivalent to gang + -er. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Gunger, West Frisian gonger, Dutch ganger, German Gänger, Danish gjænger, ganger, Swedish gängare, Icelandic gangari.
examples: Primary responsibility must rest with a ganger. He failed to appreciate the danger of disturbing the track, short of ballast, on a very hot day.

The length ganger saw the train passing with the van derailed and promptly telephoned the Sandbach signalman, who restored his signals to danger, but not in time to stop the train before the final derailment occurred.

senses: A spiritual leader in Persia, parts of Central Asia and Xinjiang, China.
Uyghur; Dungan; Hui Muslim
ety: Borrowed from Classical Persian آخُونْد (āxūnd), of unclear etymology.
examples: The Akhund of Swat, conscious of past deeds deserving of retribution, evidently conceived objects on our part beyond the punishment of the immediate offenders on the Black Mountain.

He was Khiva's akhund, or spiritual leader, who reminded the Khan that his victory had been won through treachery, and warned him that butchering the prisoners would merely worsen the crime in the eyes of God.
Yet Sayyid Akbar was a weak ruler and produced no capable heirs, at least in the opinion of the Akhund.

senses: Attractiveness; appeal, charisma.
An enticement, inducement or bait.
ety: From allure + -ment.
examples: He read the letter aloud. Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.
That though their Thoughts are ever turn'd upon appearing Aimiable, yet every Feature of their Faces and every Part of their Dress is fill'd with Snares and Allurements.
The sheer unimaginableness of coming into her mouth — of coming into anything other than the air or a tissue or a dirty sock — was an allurement too stupendous for a novice to forswear.

senses: Serving as or relating to a conclusion; concluding, postfatory.
ety: From the stem of conclusive + -ory; first attested in 1662.
examples: Finally, the conclusory section contains useful comments about the exploited learning tools and their results, whilst promising points are posed.

senses: Converging, merging or flowing together into one.
Converging, especially as viewed on a weather chart.
ety: From Latin cōnfluēns, present participle of cōnfluō.
examples: Yonder the river roll’d, whose bed, Their labyrinthine lingerings o’er, Received the confluent rills.
A confluent smallpox had in all directions flowed over his face, and left it like the complicated ribbed bed of a torrent, when the rushing waters have been dried up.

senses: Having the ability to be bent easily.
Of a person, flexible; having the ability to bend easily; resilient.
Containing many bends and twists.
Articulated.
ety: From bend + -y.
examples: Bendy rulers are far more fun than the wooden ones.

When I was in the scene in the barn he encouraged me to do as many contortions as I could, and he seemed to like the fact I was so 'bendy.' … After all how many young actresses in Hollywood are "bendy"?

senses: Different, other.
ety: Variant of an other, another, rebracketed as a nother. Compare Middle English a noþer.
examples: Executing it all well, with the feel, look and operation of a real luxury car, is a whole nother ball of wax.
He has said elfsheen four nother ways — elfsheen, elfshine, elfshone, elfshyne.
That is just a completely nother department altogether.

senses: Able to be represented by a map.
Able to be associated with something else by means of a mapping.
ety: From map + -able.
examples: Satellite imagery has made many inaccessible areas much more mappable.
Computers on the Internet are mappable to IP addresses.
This analysis suggests that the concept of homosexuality — indeed the whole notion of sexual orientation — is specific to our time and place and cannot be assumed to be mappable onto other cultures.

senses: To make the sound of water boiling on a hot surface.
To cook (something) in a manner which causes that sound.
To be exciting or dazzling.
ety: Probably a derivative of Middle English sissen (“to hiss; buzz; hum”), equivalent to siss + -le (frequentative suffix); Ultimately imitative.
examples: The sausages were sizzling on the barbecue.
I sizzled the bacon for a few minutes in the pan.

senses: The loss or return of performance-related compensation originally paid by an employer to an employee as a result of the discovery of a defect in the performance.
ety: From Latin malus, by analogy with bonus (“additional compensation”). Doublet of mal.
examples: When bank fired the loan originator, they recovered the last two years of her bonuses under the malus clause in her contract.
If the boni and mali do not depend on the frequency of claims, the average bonus-malus coefficient increases with the frequency.
If both the estimated payment- and checking-rate is not above a threshold in a district, the contracted party will receive a malus for that district, and no bonus for any other district.

senses: To discard or throw something out.
ety: From Malay buang (“throw away, discard”).
examples: Heard the Marina IR 3 Tombstones was built exactly like tombstones to buang sway for the decision makers.
I have already buanged two midterms liao.
Soon after, two other forms came into play: “anyhow whack” and “anyhow pong”. These two terms are an improvement because they buang the whole need to remember and name the action verb itself.

senses: Characteristic of bop or bebop.
ety: From bop + -y.
examples: Panic excursions to tribal Jazz wombs and transfusions Heroin nights of birth/ and soaring/ over boppy new ground.

senses: A female nix, a water-spirit.
ety: From German Nixe, feminine of Nix, from Middle High German nickes, from Old High German nihhus (“water-elf, crocodile”), from Proto-Germanic *nikwus, *nikwis, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *neygʷ- (“to wash”). Cognate with Old English nicor (“water-elf, hippopotamus, walrus”), English nicker.
examples: The place seems to have been fashioned as a dwelling for dryads and hamadryads, for nixies and pixies, and all the fabled spirits of forest and stream.
Bare from her garters up her flesh appears under the sapphire a nixie’s green.

senses: One who is therefore very wealthy, because those currency units are not hyperinflated.
One who is not wealthy (nor rare), because those currency units are hyperinflated.
Synonym of gazillionaire (“an incredibly rich person”).
ety: From trillion + -aire.
examples: The CEO of our company is a multibillionaire and now hopes to become a trillionaire.
Countless Zimbabweans had the dubious distinction of being trillionaires in 2008.
One popular foreign currency transaction scheme labelled 'burning money' made people instant quadrillionaires and trillionaires in Zimbabwean dollars.

senses: An overly inquisitive person, a nosey parker.
An act of looking at or watching something, especially something which does not directly concern the one looking.
ety: From sticky + beak; presumably from the metaphor of sticking one′s beak (“nose”) where it is not wanted (compare nosy).
examples: I walked back towards the grinning stickybeak who took a few steps backwards before fleeing for the steamy safety of his laundry.
Babies of this age are delightful stickybeaks, vitally interested in everything and everyone around them.

Vanessa took hold of his hand. ‘She′s a dear friend as well as my business manager and,’ she giggled as she admitted her agent′s greatest flaw, ‘when it comes to her clients, the world′s biggest stickybeak.’

senses: Fermented green forage fodder stored in an airtight silo or clamp.
ety: Alteration (probably by influence of silo) of ensilage (1881), itself from French ensilage, from ensiler (“put in a silo”), from Spanish ensilar.
examples: Compared to the corn silages, the sweetclover silages are much higher in digestible crude protein, but lower in total digestible nutrients.

senses: A small hill.
ety: From Middle English hillok, equivalent to hill + -ock.
examples: As he rounded a hillock, he perceived that the roadway was now a crying mass of wagons, teams, and men.
Just upstream of Dryburgh Abbey, a reproduction of a classical Greek temple stands at the top of a wooded hillock on the river’s north bank.

senses: narrow-brimmed type of felt hat, described as having a "shorter brim which is angled down at the front and slightly turned up at the back" in comparison to the fedora
ety: From the stage adaptation of George du Maurier's novel Trilby, in which such hats were worn.
examples: Billy was seventeen years old. He was wearing a new navy-blue overcoat, a new brown trilby hat, and a new brown suit, and he was feeling fine.

senses: A member of a Serbian royalist army band.
An adherent of a nationalist revival of the historical Chetnik movement.
ety: From Serbo-Croatian četnik, from četa (“band, group”) + -nik.
examples: Since most Chetniks only wanted to fight close to their homes, a mobile army that could carry out sustained campaigns under central command never developed.

senses: A female prophet.
ety: From Middle English prophetesse, from Old French prophetesse, from Late Latin prophetissa. By surface analysis, prophet + -ess.
examples: What made matters worse was that Montanus was accompanied by female prophetesses who spoke in states of ecstasy.

senses: Lacking education or knowledge; unenlightened; also, lacking morality; immoral, unscrupulous.
ety: From benight + -ed.
examples: It seems quite possible, however, that the roots of the Western's decline lie deeper than in the likes and animadversions of benighted critics. The Western has lost its audience.

senses: Agricultural labour; husbandry.
The state of being tilled, or prepared for a crop; culture.
Cultivated land
Rich cultivated soil.
ety: From Middle English tilthe, from Old English tilþ, tilþe, corresponding to till + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
examples: The land is in good tilth and ready to plant.
Escaped from thicket and from fen at last he saw the tilth of men.
One morning she was kneeling on an old grain sack on the wet black soil, turning the thick rich tilth over and smoothing it ready for the new lettuces.

senses: A flight past a celestial object in order to make observations.
A low-level ceremonial flight, typically in connection with an airshow or a military parade.
A brief visit.
ety: Deverbal from fly by.
examples: The upcoming flyby of Halley's comet is expected to provide new information on the nature of the comet.
Farthest from the dim red dwarf Ondeste, the ice dwarf Maisuth has attracted no interest beyond a cursory flyby by automated probe in 1874. No significant resources were noted.
